items.abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

items.summary: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. items.abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

items.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

items.abstract: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

items.abstract: Task-based fMRI of the cervical spinal cord is limited by physiological noise and small sample sizes. The primary objective of this study was to examine whether a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based denoising framework can improve the detection of task-dependent functional connectivity between cervical spinal segments using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis. An open dataset of 26 healthy adults performing a hand-grasp task with alternating right- and left-hand blocks during 3 T fMRI was analyzed. A CNN with Inception V3 transfer learning (91.0% slice-level and 89.2% block-level accuracy) was trained to classify grasp versus rest, and the trained model was then utilized to derive denoised time series from masks of the spinal segments C5-C8. A gPPI model with a C6 ventral horn seed was evaluated using FDR correction and permutation testing (n = 1000). C6 showed positive task-dependent connectivity with C7 (β = 0.72, p = 0.003) and C8 (β = 0.58, p = 0.018), and negative connectivity with C5 (β = -0.31, p = 0.041), which is broadly consistent with the organization of the cervical myotomes. The C6-C5 effect was marginal and was not detected when conventional time series were used (p = 0.21), and therefore it requires replication. Grad-CAM maps aligned with ventral horn motor pools (Dice = 0.89 at C7). These results suggest that deep learning-based denoising may increase the sensitivity of spinal cord fMRI to segmental connectivity, although validation in larger cohorts is needed.

items.abstract: Radiation dose in medical imaging has been quantified through measurable metrics such as computed tomography dose index volume (CTDIvol), dose length product (DLP), kerma area product, kerma at reference point etc. They are benchmarked through diagnostic reference levels (DRLs); and communicated in terms of effective dose and population-based risk estimates. None of these tools was designed to describe the dose, the reference standard, or the risk applicable to the individual patient. In every other domain of medicine where a potentially harmful agent accompanies a beneficial clinical intervention, from contrast nephrotoxicity in CT imaging to anesthetic risk in surgery, the field has moved beyond population metrics to individualized measurement and individual clinical decision-making. Radiation protection in medical imaging has not yet made this transition. This paper resolves several open questions on cumulative dose that have long been used to justify inaction. It argues that the transition is now technically achievable, that the barriers to it are primarily architectural, regulatory, and cultural rather than physical or computational, and that artificial intelligence and emerging imaging technologies provide the enabling infrastructure to complete it. We describe the three-tier structure of barriers to individual dose tracking: technical, institutional and regulatory, and cultural; and propose the elements of a system that would place the individual patient's cumulative radiation dose record where it belongs: in their medical record, alongside their medication list, visible at the point of every subsequent clinical imaging decision.

items.abstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T 1 , T 2 , diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T 1 and T 2 ), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

items.abstract: Background Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in multiple organs. Although brain MRI screening is recommended in all patients with HHT, in many centers, this may be difficult to implement due to organizational constraints. The aim of this study was to develop a machine learning model to predict the presence of bAVMs and other cerebrovascular malformations in patients with HHT, with the goal of supporting risk stratification in centers where genotype information is already available and identifying patients who may benefit from closer and more conservative surveillance. Methods All patients with confirmed diagnosis of HHT, complete genetic work-up, and radiological screening (2018-2026) were included for the analysis. Two end points were defined: probability of detecting bAVMs, and probability of detecting any cerebrovascular findings. Analysis was performed using Python and R. Results A total of 142 patients with confirmed HHT (meeting ≥ 3 Curaçao criteria) were included. For bAVM prediction, both models showed good discrimination, with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.73-0.94) for Logistic Regression (LR) and 0.85 (95% CI: 0.74-0.96) for Random Forest (RF). Despite the slightly higher AUC, RF showed lower specificity, PPV, and F1 score, higher sensitivity (0.73 vs. 0.69) and same NPV. LR also showed better calibration, with an intercept of -0.30 (95% CI: -1.38-0.78) and slope of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.34-1.40), compared with 1.39 (95% CI: -0.46-3.23) and 2.39 (95% CI: 0.64-4.15), respectively, for RF. In contrast, models predicting overall cerebrovascular malformations showed limited discrimination and poor calibration with both LR and RF. For bAVM prediction, LR identified deletion mutations, ENG, family history, ACVRL1, and truncated variants as the most influential features, while RF SHAP analysis highlighted ACVRL1, ENG, age, pulmonary AVMs, and family history. Conclusion Effective risk stratification was achieved by the phenotype-specific bAVM model, supporting its potential applicability. Upon external validation this tool may enable an efficient allocation of screening strategies.

items.abstract: Objectives To develop TotalSpineSeg, a robust tool for vertebrae and intervertebral disc instance segmentation, along with spinal cord and spinal canal segmentation, capable of processing any 3D medical image regardless of contrast, resolution, or field of view, while overcoming fusion and fragmentation errors common in standard segmentation. Materials and methods A two-stage cascaded deep learning model was trained on 1404 MRIs. To explicitly prevent errors where adjacent vertebrae merge or a single vertebra splits, the architecture employs a novel "odd/even" representation. The second stage is conditioned on an odd-intervertebral disc mask from the first stage to assign distinct semantic classes to alternating vertebrae, enforcing accurate separation between neighboring vertebrae. Finally, a landmark-based logic uses key anatomical points (C2-C3, C7-T1, T12-L1, and L5-S) to anchor sequential labeling, while a localizer-based strategy ensures accurate identification even in truncated, short field-of-view scans. Results Evaluation across diverse contrasts and pathologies yielded a vertebral identification rate of 96.22% on localizer MRI and generalized to CT scans with a 92.87% identification rate. For intervertebral disc instance labeling, where vertebral separation is not mandatory, both model stages attained 99% labeling accuracy with a mean positional L2 error of 1.55 mm, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Conclusion TotalSpineSeg successfully generalizes to diverse 3D medical images, overcoming variations in contrast, resolution, and field of view. The proposed topological constraints effectively eliminate vertebral fusion and fragmentation errors, delivering a state-of-the-art identification rate for both vertebrae and intervertebral discs across MRI and CT modalities. Key points Question Can a topology-constrained framework overcome heterogeneous contrasts and resolution limits, including localizers, to ensure robust, automated vertebral and disc labeling? Findings TotalSpineSeg achieved a high identification rate across diverse contrasts, localizers, and CT, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by eliminating fusion and fragmentation errors. Clinical relevance TotalSpineSeg enables fully automated biomarker extraction from clinical scans, allowing precise assessment of stenosis, lesions, and atrophy against normative ranges.

items.abstract: Endolymphatic hydrops MRI is used for the diagnostic evaluation of patients with primary or secondary endolymphatic hydrops. Delayed intravenous post-Gd 3-dimensional fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (3D-FLAIR) and 3-dimensional real inversion recovery (3D-real IR) sequences are the most widely applied techniques, because they exploit subtle Gd-related signal differences between perilymph and endolymph. Yet image quality and diagnostic confidence depend on protocol design, and variation persists between institutions, scanners, and vendors. This educational review provides a visually oriented, practical framework for optimising endolymphatic hydrops MRI, focusing on three core determinants: acquisition parameters, post-processing strategies, and contrast-agent selection. The physical principles underlying key sequence-parameter choices are explained, including the use of long echo trains to maximise acquisition efficiency, prolonged repetition times to enhance the perilymphatic signal, and inversion times tailored to the selected repetition time to achieve effective suppression of the endolymphatic signal. Representative graphs and imaging examples illustrate how protocol modifications influence contrast and diagnostic performance. The review further discusses post-processing approaches and emerging artificial intelligence-based techniques, including deep learning reconstruction, as tools to improve image quality, shorten scan time, or support higher spatial resolution. Finally, the role of gadolinium-based contrast agents, scan delay, and clinical protocol design is also addressed. Four-hour delayed intravenous imaging remains the current standard, although sequence-specific timing, single- or two-step protocols, and half-dose high-relaxivity agents may offer opportunities for tailored imaging, reduced Gd exposure, and improved sustainability. By linking sequence principles to practical protocol choices, this review aims to support reproducible, high-quality hydrops MRI across clinical settings. KEY POINTS: Question Optimisation and standardisation of 3D-FLAIR and 3D-real IR protocols are essential for accurate, reproducible assessment of endolymphatic hydrops across institutions, scanner platforms, and vendors. Findings Use TE 500-700 ms and a long echo train for efficiency/background suppression, TR ~ 16,000 ms to enhance perilymph, and TI 2400-3000 ms to suppress endolymph. Critical relevance statement Emerging deep-learning reconstruction techniques may shorten acquisition times or improve spatial resolution, while half-dose, high-relaxivity GBCAs may provide hydrops visualisation comparable to higher-dose conventional contrast protocols.

items.abstract: This retrospective single-center study evaluated segment-level agreement between experienced cardiac radiologists and a research AI platform for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Asymptomatic individuals undergoing CCTA at a health screening center were studied, excluding those with prior revascularization, coronary anomaly, or total occlusion. Stenosis grade and plaque composition were independently assessed by the AI platform and two cardiac radiologists at the segment level, with disagreements between the two radiologists resolved by consensus. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen's κ, quadratic weighted κ for ordinal grading, observed agreement, and positive and negative agreement for dichotomized significant stenosis. The cohort comprised 172 participants and 2,582 segments. Significant stenosis was uncommon (18/2,582, 0.7%), with moderate agreement (κ = 0.412; observed agreement 98.5%; positive agreement 0.418; negative agreement 0.992). Agreement was fair for ordinal stenosis grade (κ = 0.397; quadratic weighted κ = 0.573; observed agreement 84.0%) and plaque composition (κ = 0.330; observed agreement 81.8%). Stenosis-grade agreement was lower in plaque-containing than plaque-free segments, an exploratory finding given marked differences in subgroup size and prevalence. Myocardial bridging and image quality were not major descriptive determinants of discordance. In this low-prevalence cohort, AI-based CCTA analysis showed high negative agreement for radiologist-defined significant stenosis but limited concordance for grading and plaque characterization. Reflecting low prevalence and few positive cases, the findings do not establish independent rule-out performance but support prospective evaluation of AI as an expert-supervised pre-reading or triage adjunct, with positive, ambiguous, or plaque-containing findings requiring expert review.

items.abstract: Objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the techniques and reported patterns of heatmap-based visual explanations in deep learning (DL) systems for dental radiographic classification tasks. Methods A literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore Library, Oria.no and Google Scholar to retrieve studies using DL for dental classification tasks. Only articles with a visual explanation (heatmap) were selected. Risk of bias assessment was done with QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI and CEBM. The heatmap technique, reasons for inclusion, explanations provided and patterns were analysed. Results In the 136 studies reviewed, Grad-CAM was the most commonly used technique. The predominant reason for using visual explanations was to understand the decision-making process of the DL model. Some heatmaps reflect established radiographic criteria, while others exhibit unique, label-dependent patterns that sometimes emphasise irrelevant areas. Cropping to the region of interest influences visual explanations. Conclusions Visual explanations seem clinically plausible to domain experts when aligned with domain knowledge, but clinical plausibility does not equal technical faithfulness. Formal faithfulness testing was rarely performed among the included studies. Therefore, explanations should not be assumed to accurately represent the model's underlying reasoning. Limitations include the evaluation of studies not primarily designed for visual explanation assessment. No funding was received for this review. Authors declare no competing interests. Advances in knowledge Visual explanations, while clinically plausible when aligned with domain knowledge, remain insufficiently validated and should not be assumed to faithfully represent model reasoning. An implausible explanation does not necessarily indicate model failure. Domain/task-specific evaluation metrics for explainable AI in dentomaxillofacial radiology are needed.

items.abstract: Objectives Although the precise mechanism underlying activation of Spo0A needs to be clarified to fully understand C. perfringens sporulation, the molecules directly interacting with Spo0A have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify proteins interacting with Spo0A during C. perfringens sporulation by a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay. Methods Prey libraries constructed using the genomes of C. perfringens SM101 and str. 13 and a bait plasmid encoding the receiver domain of Spo0A in C. perfringens SM101 were used for Y2H assay. The deletion mutant and its complemented strain were constructed by homologous recombination. Phenotypic analyses included measurements of bacterial growth, sporulation efficiency, cell morphology, mRNA expression of sporulation-related genes, and the amount of phosphorylated Spo0A. Potential protein interactions were evaluated using AlphaFold 3. Results Y2H screening identified CPR0186, a hypothetical protein in C. perfringens SM101, as a Spo0A-interacting candidate, and AlphaFold 3 modeling supported the possibility of the direct interaction with the receiver domain of Spo0A. The cpr0186-null mutant exhibited growth comparable to that of the wild-type strain, but showed significantly reduced sporulation. The mutant also showed significantly decreased mRNA expression of spo0A, sigF, sigE, sigG, and sigK. No apparent difference in the ratio of Spo0A∼P to unphosphorylated Spo0A was observed among the strains under the conditions tested. Conclusion cpr0186 promotes sporulation in C. perfringens SM101 and is suggested to contribute to the expression of Spo0A-regulated genes. CPR0186 may interact directly with Spo0A although the functional significance of this interaction remains to be determined.

items.abstract: Snakebite envenoming remains a major public health problem in Latin America. Although antivenoms are produced by many Latin American manufacturers, their use in accidents involving heterologous snake species or from different geographic areas requires preclinical testing, typically conducted in experimental animals. Here, we assessed whether toxin-centered in silico analyses can predict antivenom efficacy by evaluating the performance of the Instituto Butantan Bothrops antivenom against venoms from medically relevant Ecuadorian Bothrops asper, B. atrox, and B. bilineatus. We combined transcriptome-guided proteomics, toxin phylogeny, AlphaFold-based structural modeling, and DiscoTope epitope mapping to compare Ecuadorian venom toxins with those in the immunization mixture used for antivenom production. Although toxin abundance and composition varied among venoms, most Ecuadorian toxins had close orthologs in the immunization mixture, and most predicted epitope residues were conserved or showed conservative substitutions, suggesting broad antibody recognition. Divergent toxins, particularly some PLA 2 s, PI-class SVMPs, SVSPs, and CTLs, showed non-conservative substitutions that could reduce antibody binding. Experimental validation supported these predictions: ELISA and Western blotting showed strong antivenom reactivity, while in vivo assays demonstrated complete neutralization of lethality and hemorrhagic activity, with partial limitations against B. asper myotoxicity and the defibrinogenating activity induced by B. asper and B. atrox. These findings indicate that epitope-focused in silico approaches can support antivenom efficacy assessment and guide antivenom improvement while reducing reliance on animal testing. Moreover, we demonstrated that the Instituto Butantan Bothrops antivenom effectively neutralizes the lethality and specific toxic activities of important medically relevant venoms from Bothrops snakes in Ecuador.

items.abstract: Missense variants in glycan-related genes (glycogenes) underlie many congenital disorders of glycosylation and related conditions, yet a large fraction remain classified as variants of uncertain significance. Because glycogenes often show low evolutionary conservation, conventional sequence-based predictors are frequently uninformative, making structure-based interpretation particularly valuable. This review examines how structure-based and glycosylation-aware approaches can improve the interpretation of glycogene variants. Advances in protein structure prediction, notably AlphaFold, now allow variant-induced structural perturbations to be assessed proteome-wide using structure-derived features such as solvent accessibility, thermodynamic stability (ΔΔG), and local model confidence (pLDDT). Such structural features can be combined to predict the impact of glycogene variants, as exemplified by VarMeter and VarMeter2, which have successfully identified pathogenic missense variants of arylsulfatase L (ARSL) and N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase (SGSH) in patients with undiagnosed disease. Despite the progress in these tools, there remain challenges especially relevant to glycobiology, including the limited accuracy of current ΔΔG predictors, the distinct behavior of gain-of-function and stabilizing variants, the need for proteome-scale computation, and the critical but still underexplored contribution of protein glycosylation to structural stability. We argue that incorporating glycosylation into structural energetics is a key next step toward more accurate, glyco-aware variant interpretation.

items.abstract: Introduction Nanoparticle drug delivery systems (NP DDS) have transformed therapeutic delivery by improving drug stability, extending circulation time, and enabling targeted biodistribution. However, clinical translation remains limited by protein corona formation, immune recognition, and accelerated blood clearance following repeated administration. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has been the gold-standard antifouling material for decades, but emerging anti-PEG immune responses have driven the search for alternative stealth technologies. Areas covered Zwitterionic peptides (ZIPs) have emerged as a promising class of antifouling materials because they combine the hydration-mediated stealth properties of zwitterionic polymers with the molecular precision and programmability of peptide synthesis. Here, ZIP applications in drug delivery were reviewed using the Web of Science database from 2014-2026, focusing on reducing and controlling the protein corona, recent advances in ZIP-based drug delivery, and the potential of high-throughput screening platforms and machine learning-guided ZIP design. Recent studies suggest that biological interactions of ZIP-functionalized NPs are governed primarily by charge motifs rather than precise sequences, creating new opportunities for material design. Expert opinion This observation motivates developing semi-randomized ZIPs (srZIPs) that preserve charge organization while introducing sequence diversity. By maintaining key physicochemical and biological properties while diversifying composition, srZIPs may reduce immune recognition without sacrificing antifouling function.

items.abstract: Objectives To synthesize evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled postoperative pain assessment and prediction, opioid-related risk prediction, patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) monitoring, and implementation considerations in pediatric surgical care. Design A systematic review with narrative synthesis of evidence concerning AI applications in pediatric postoperative pain management and opioid stewardship. Data sources Biomedical, nursing, engineering, computer science, trial-registry, Google Scholar, and citation sources were systematically searched through March 2026. Review/analysis methods Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, multimodal sensing, or AI-enabled tools in pediatric surgical or postoperative populations. A single reviewer performed study selection, data extraction, and methodological appraisal, with consultation from an external subject-matter expert. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using design-appropriate appraisal tools. Findings were narratively synthesized because clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results Of 198 identified records, 137 were screened, and 20 full-text reports were assessed. Eleven studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, alongside one companion dataset report. Applications included automated pain assessment, home-based pain monitoring, prolonged opioid-use prediction, and prediction of pain or adverse effects during PCA. Most studies evaluated facial expressions using computer vision or multimodal combinations of physiological, video, and audio data. Reported performance varied substantially, with validation predominantly limited to internal datasets. No randomized trial or controlled clinical-impact study demonstrated reductions in pain intensity, opioid exposure or prescribing, adverse events, readmissions, or length of stay attributable to AI-guided care. Conclusions AI-enabled tools show potential to support pediatric postoperative pain assessment and opioid-related risk stratification. However, current evidence is insufficient to justify routine clinical implementation. External validation, prospective clinical evaluation, fairness assessment, and workflow-integrated effectiveness studies are needed. Nursing practice implications AI-enabled assessment and prediction tools may complement pediatric nurses' clinical assessment, pain monitoring, opioid-related risk identification, patient and family education, and timely escalation of care. Nevertheless, their use should remain supplementary to professional nursing judgment until clinical effectiveness, safety, and generalizability are established.

items.abstract: Background Voice disorders can substantially impair communication and quality of life, creating a need for reliable, non-invasive, and reproducible approaches for automated voice assessment. Conventional acoustic features such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) have been widely used for voice-disorder classification, but their ability to represent the frequency selectivity and nonlinear characteristics of human auditory processing may be limited. Auditory-inspired representations derived from cochlear modeling may provide complementary information for distinguishing pathological voice patterns. Objectives This study investigates the effectiveness of three acoustic representations, namely Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), Gammatone Filterbank Cepstral Coefficients (GTFCC), and Gammachirp Filterbank Cepstral Coefficients (GCFCC), in combination with different convolutional neural network architectures for multiclass voice-disorder classification. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluating these representations under a strict speaker-independent validation protocol designed to reduce the risk of speaker leakage. Methods Experiments were conducted using a subset of the Saarbrücken Voice Database (SVD) comprising 3022 recordings from 262 speakers, representing seven diagnostic categories: healthy voice, functional dysphonia, laryngitis, leukoplakia, psychogenic dysphonia, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, and spasmodic dysphonia. All recordings were converted to mono, resampled to 16 kHz, band-pass filtered between 80 Hz and 8 kHz, amplitude-normalized, and temporally standardized to 300 frames using truncation or zero-padding. Three feature representations were extracted: MFCC, GTFCC based on an ERB-spaced Gammatone filterbank, and GCFCC based on Gammachirp auditory filtering. Each representation comprised 13 cepstral coefficients together with their first- and second-order temporal derivatives, resulting in 39 × 300 time-frequency feature maps. These representations were evaluated using a custom convolutional neural network, VGG16-BN, and ResNet-50. A speaker-independent five-fold cross-validation strategy was employed. All recordings from the same speaker were assigned to a single fold and remained within a single partition throughout the evaluation. Within each fold, data augmentation and class balancing were applied exclusively to the training partition, while validation and test recordings remained unaltered. The augmented training data were generated using controlled Gaussian-noise injection and pitch shifting, followed by targeted augmentation of underrepresented classes. Classification performance was assessed using accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score, together with 95% confidence intervals and fold-level variability. Statistical comparisons between feature representations were performed using paired t tests with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Results Across the evaluated architectures, the cochlear-inspired representations generally provided higher classification performance than conventional MFCCs, with GCFCC yielding the strongest overall performance. The best-performing configuration was ResNet-50 combined with GCFCC, achieving a mean accuracy of 94.77% (95% CI: 94.36 to 95.18%), with fold-wise accuracies ranging from 94.43% to 95.17%. The corresponding macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score were 94.46% (95% CI: 93.81 to 95.10%), 94.94% (95% CI: 94.35 to 95.53%), and 94.67% (95% CI: 94.31 to 95.03%), respectively. The coefficient of variation for accuracy was 0.35%, indicating relatively low inter-fold variability under the speaker-independent evaluation protocol. Statistical analysis further supported the advantage of GCFCC over GTFCC and MFCC for accuracy across the evaluated architectures, although not all differences in macro-averaged F1-score reached statistical significance after multiple-comparison correction. Conclusions The findings indicate that cochlear-inspired cepstral representations, particularly GCFCC, can provide useful acoustic information for multiclass voice-disorder classification when combined with deep residual learning. The strict speaker-independent evaluation and training-only augmentation provide a conservative estimate of performance within the evaluated SVD subset. However, the results should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical diagnostic capability. External validation on independent databases, additional speaking conditions and languages, connected speech, and prospective clinical cohorts is required to determine the generalizability and clinical utility of the proposed framework.

items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy faces a critical clinical hurdle: cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Current CRS management strategies have limited selectivity and may interfere with CAR-T cell antitumor activity, highlighting the need for more targeted and precisely controllable interventions. Nanoengineering offers a promising approach to address these limitations by enabling the spatiotemporally controlled monitoring and modulation of inflammatory responses, with the potential to mitigate excessive cytokine release while preserving CAR-T cell therapeutic efficacy, driving a paradigm shift toward programmable, proactive immune regulation. This review systematically examines nanointervention strategies for mitigating CAR-T-induced CRS, including molecular monitoring, cytokine clearance, targeted delivery, stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic designs, and genetic reprogramming. These approaches enable precise intervention across multiple stages-from early inflammation detection and localized neutralization to source-level cellular engineering. Finally, we discuss challenges in biosafety, clinical translation, and the potential of artificial intelligence-driven predictive platforms. Nanotechnology offers a transformative pathway to redefine CRS from an unpredictable complication into a manageable therapeutic window, paving the way for safer next-generation cellular immunotherapies.

items.abstract: Background Heart failure is classically divided into two subtypes based on the ejection fraction (EF): HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), each with varying risk mitigation strategies. Electrocardiogram-based artificial intelligence (AI) may facilitate HF subtype-specific risk prediction, to enable tailored prevention. Methods and results Based on a previously validated HF prediction architecture, we developed an ECG-based AI model to predict 10-year risk of incident HFrEF (LVEF <50%) versus HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%) (Electrocardiogram to Heart Failure Subtype, "ECG2HF-Subtype"). ECG2HF-Subtype was developed in 98,190 individuals in Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), and validated in three test sets: MGH, Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH), and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), among individuals without prior HF. HF was identified using a validated natural language processing model, and subtypes were classified by LVEF proximate to incident HF. Discrimination was quantified using time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP), with comparisons to age and sex, and a multinomial logistic regression classifier including PREVENT-HF variables. In aggregate, models were evaluated in MGH (n=16,739, age 56±17, 54% women), BWH (n=75,195, 56±16, 59%) and BIDMC (n=30,133, 56±17, 54%). ECG2HF-Subtype consistently discriminated incident HFrEF (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.89 [0.86-0.91], 10-year AP: 0.11 [95%CI 0.09-0.15], cumulative incidence 1.73%; BWH: 0.88 [0.87-0.89], 0.13 [0.11-0.14], 2.23% BIDMC: 0.88 [0.86-0.89], 0.14 [0.12-0.17], 2.19%) and HFpEF events (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.83 [0.81-0.85], 10-year AP: 0.10 [95% CI 0.09-0.13], cumulative incidence 3.17%; BWH: 0.79 [0.77-0.80], 0.06 [0.06-0.07], 2.75%), BIDMC: 0.81 [0.80-0.82], 0.10 [0.09-0.12], 3.49%), with consistently greater AUROC versus age and sex. When compared to PREVENT-HF variables, ECG2HF-Subtypes had favorable discrimination of HFrEF (e.g., 10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.86 [0.84-0.88] vs. 0.78 [0.76-0.80]), and modestly lower for HFpEF (10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.78 [0.76-0.80] vs. 0.81 [0.79-0.82]). Conclusions By predicting risk of HFpEF and HFrEF, AI-enabled ECG analysis may enable targeted prevention to reduce HF-related morbidity.

items.abstract: Sustained adherence to intraocular pressure-lowering medications is essential for preventing progressive visual loss in patients with glaucoma on pharmacotherapy. However, adherence remains suboptimal across patient populations as the result of cognitive, behavioural, physical, and socioeconomic barriers. Recent advances in digital health have introduced smartphone-based adherence supports intended to reinforce glaucoma medication routines, improve treatment organization, and support self-management. This narrative review synthesises evidence examining smartphone-based reminder applications and related digital adherence supports in glaucoma care, with attention to usability, patient experience, behavioural determinants, and clinical feasibility. Preliminary studies have reported improvements in short-term self-reported adherence and glaucoma-specific quality of life, particularly among patients with low baseline adherence. However, reminder-based interventions may provide only temporary benefit if they do not address broader structural, behavioural, and situational barriers to adherence. Current evidence remains limited by short follow-up durations, reliance on self-reported adherence measures, and limited evaluation of long-term clinical outcomes such as intraocular pressure stability and visual field preservation. Digital adherence tools may therefore be most effective when integrated alongside broader behavioural and relationship-based support strategies, including patient education, clinician communication, and caregiver involvement. Emerging technologies such as automated messaging systems and artificial intelligence-assisted tools may represent future directions for adherence support, although evidence in glaucoma remains limited. Further research is required to establish personalised, durable, and equitable adherence support frameworks in glaucoma care.

items.abstract: High-throughput technologies now make it possible to simultaneously generate genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data. Spatial and single-cell platforms, in turn, provide cellular and spatial information in greater detail. Relying on a single omics method captures only a fraction of this complexity and often overlooks interactions across different layers. Despite these advances, clinical applications remain limited. This review examines integration strategies, along with their applications in various diseases, and the machine learning methods used to implement them. Rather than focusing solely on predictive performance, the aim is to support biological reasoning by formulating testable hypotheses, drawing causal inferences, and gaining insights that can guide clinical decisions. A reanalysis of a publicly available chronic lymphocytic leukemia dataset revealed that one data type was missing in approximately one-third of patients. When early and intermediate integration were combined with simple zero imputation, agreement dropped to chance and near-chance levels. In contrast, late integration, which does not require data imputation, was largely unaffected by this issue. This demonstrates that findings regarding integration strategies cannot be considered in isolation from how missing data are handled. The review also covers approaches that directly address missing data. Major barriers to clinical application include confounding batch effects, unreliable feature attribution when features are correlated, and deficiencies in clinical quality assurance. This review proposes four criteria to help identify models that not only ensure statistical validity but also genuinely support biological reasoning: mechanistic specificity, causal grounding, failure transparency, and decision relevance.

items.abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

items.summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. items.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

items.summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. items.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

items.abstract: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising posterior is viewed through the lens of scoring rules, the path derivative of a kernel scoring rule defined by the noise potential recovers the Stein score of the noisy marginal. Thus, the familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedie's formula is lifted to a distributional correspondence between Gibbs noise distributions, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, which gives a Tweedie-style relation for each noise potential. Among its consequences, this identity gives a posterior-samples-to-score route to score estimation, yields a principled criterion for estimating unknown noise parameters, and enables diffusion-style sampling along user-chosen paths through the noise-parameter space, supplying the score-based perspective on recent generative methods trained with scoring rules.

items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding…
items.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

items.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

items.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
items.summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to…
items.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

items.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
items.summary: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol…
items.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

items.abstract: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.

items.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

items.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.

items.abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

items.title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
items.summary: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow.
