items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46times to 10.87times with one request, and from 1.94times to 3.93times with batching.

items.title: MoviEdit: Long-form Multi-Shot Video Editing Made Easy
items.summary: Long-form multi-shot video editing requires an intended edit to remain coherent across abrupt changes in scene, viewpoint, and subject appearance, while processing substantially longer visual context than conventional single-shot editors. We introduce MoviEdit, an end-to-end framework for scalable long-form multi-shot video editing that jointly addresses the challenges of data, modeling, and evaluation. To provide…
items.abstract: Long-form multi-shot video editing requires an intended edit to remain coherent across abrupt changes in scene, viewpoint, and subject appearance, while processing substantially longer visual context than conventional single-shot editors. We introduce MoviEdit, an end-to-end framework for scalable long-form multi-shot video editing that jointly addresses the challenges of data, modeling, and evaluation. To provide cross-shot supervision data at scale, we develop automatic data-generation pipelines spanning synchronized multi-view footage, real-world multi-shot videos, and generated multi-shot content, yielding 87K paired editing videos without manual annotation. Architecturally, MoviEdit employs a cascaded bidirectional-autoregressive design: a lightweight bidirectional stage first establishes a globally coherent editing draft over a spatiotemporally compressed representation, which is then autoregressively propagated and refined over the full video. We further introduce MoviEdit-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for systematic evaluation of long-form multi-shot video editing. Extensive experiments show that MoviEdit substantially outperforms existing open-source models and performs on par with industry frontier models across text-guided and image-guided editing. Visit our project page for complete results and to access the benchmark: https://multi-shot-edit.github.io/

items.title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
items.summary: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while…
items.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: https://xiaokunsun.github.io/SeMo3D.github.io/.

items.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
items.summary: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five…
items.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

items.title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?
items.summary: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026.…
items.abstract: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.

items.title: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models
items.summary: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end…
items.abstract: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end multimodal DR agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit, operating over a corpus of 1.06M pages. To evaluate this setting, we construct DRPixelBench, a benchmark on scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. Surprisingly, page-native DR already works well without training, outperforming OCR-based baselines across state-of-the-art models like GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B, while requiring fewer tool calls. We next turn to DR training. A key challenge is that teacher trajectories for agentic supervised finetuning are noisy, mixing critical reasoning and action steps with redundant or failed attempts. To address this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, a fine-grained credit assignment method that weights individual reasoning and action steps by their counterfactual contribution to the final answer. Our training improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points on DRPixelBench, and likewise outperforms the untrained baseline on four existing benchmarks. On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, DR Pixel comes within 1.8 points of an oracle that is given the gold pages directly. Our results suggest that the conventional OCR-then-retrieve pipeline is not only unnecessary but suboptimal: directly retrieving and reasoning over visual document pages makes complex DR both more effective and more efficient.

items.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a…
items.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

items.summary: AI-generated videos often depict people within detailed scenes while leaving their small facial regions poorly resolved. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within a reference-guided video flow model. Source--noise mixing…
items.abstract: AI-generated videos often depict people within detailed scenes while leaving their small facial regions poorly resolved. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within a reference-guided video flow model. Source--noise mixing initializes reconstruction from a partially preserved observation, and structured reference injection separates appearance anchors from continuous motion context. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources under target audio. Appearance and synchronization supervision allow the model to recover facial detail and support visual dubbing when the audio is replaced. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the best paired perceptual similarity and synchronization scores among the compared restoration methods. Component comparisons examine audio conditioning, the reconstruction formulation, and reference injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage. injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage.

items.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360^{circ} View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments
items.summary: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360^{circ} scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware…
items.abstract: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360^{circ} scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360^{circ} panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. Project page: https://ntuneillee.github.io/research/photoguider/

items.title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
items.summary: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an…
items.abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.

items.title: Decoding antibody-antigen recognition: the BL8 language and its application in calibrating deep learning predictions
items.summary: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic…
items.abstract: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic when evaluating the massive and frequently overconfident structural hypotheses generated by modern deep learning models. Here, we introduce BL8, an interpretable, eight-view structural language that comprehensively parameterizes interfaces across topology, shape, interaction, CDR conformation, flexibility, interfacial area, amino-acid-pair composition, and sequence background. Using 15,396 experimental interface records from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), we built a fixed reference atlas containing 1,498 discrete BL8 signatures. The atlas shows that natural interfaces occupy a diverse, long-tailed structural space in which similar geometric scaffolds can be associated with different chemical and sequence features. Furthermore, we projected 28,501 predicted complexes involving programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), generated using AlphaFold 3 (AF3), Protenix-v2, and OpenDDE, into the reference space. Acting as a robust underlying calibration layer, BL8 successfully decoupled physical viability from native confidence illusions, revealing cross-target hallucinations and filtering out 15.3% to 20.1% of highly deceptive false-positive predictions. Crucially, by benchmarking distinct generative behaviors across models, it enabled the extraction of highly reliable, multi-model consensus out-of-distribution binding paradigms. Together, BL8 bridges foundational biophysics with large-scale computational predictions, providing an essential benchmarking framework for discovering novel mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence. Highlights BL8 encodes antibody–antigen interfaces through eight interpretable views. An atlas of 15,396 interfaces defines 1,498 experimental BL8 signatures. BL8 reveals long-tailed diversity in antibody–antigen recognition. BL8 rejects 15.3%–20.1% of high-confidence false-positive predictions. Cross-model consensus prioritizes candidate binding modes beyond the atlas.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models. ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/ . Abstract Figure

items.abstract: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) prediction plays a central role in modern computer-aided drug discovery by enabling early evaluation of pharmacokinetic behaviour and safety liabilities. This tutorial presents a reproducible computational workflow for large-scale ADMET profiling using ADMET-AI 2.0, a graph neural network-based prediction platform, applied to 200 cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) inhibitors curated from ChEMBL release 35. Implemented within an annotated Jupyter notebook, the workflow integrates cheminformatics preprocessing, physicochemical property analysis, drug-likeness evaluation, structural alert screening, absorption and distribution profiling, CYP450-mediated metabolism prediction, excretion assessment, toxicity evaluation, Tox21 pathway analysis, DrugBank percentile benchmarking, and composite multi-parameter optimisation scoring. A total of 104 ADMET-related outputs were generated per compound, including 52 predictive endpoints and 52 corresponding DrugBank approved-drug percentile rankings. The 200 curated CDK2 inhibitors exhibited 100% Lipinski Ro5 compliance, 38.5% predicted CYP3A4 inhibition, 73.5% predicted hERG liability, and 99.5% predicted DILI risk, with a mean composite ADMET score of 0.46 and a mean traffic light green flag count of 9.5/13. The workflow provides an accessible and FAIR-compliant framework for ADMET analysis, cheminformatics education, and reproducible computational drug discovery.Scientific contributionThis work contributes a structured educational framework for teaching and implementing computational ADMET analysis in modern drug discovery. To be explicit about the nature of this contribution: the novelty is pedagogical and integrative rather than methodological, no new prediction model, algorithm, or endpoint is introduced. The study demonstrates how an existing graph neural network-based prediction model (ADMET-AI) can be integrated with open-source cheminformatics workflows to support interpretable and reproducible pharmacokinetic assessment. Beyond endpoint prediction, the tutorial emphasises practical data handling, workflow automation, compound prioritisation, and transparent result interpretation within a Jupyter notebook environment. The inclusion of DrugBank percentile benchmarking, traffic-light visualisation, and composite scoring strategies provides learners and researchers with practical, worked examples of established multi-parameter decision-making approaches during lead optimisation, rather than new decision frameworks in their own right. By combining methodological clarity with FAIR and reproducible research principles, the workflow serves as a scalable resource for cheminformatics education, computational pharmacology training, and ADMET-guided drug development studies.

items.abstract: Antibody drug development is a years-long, costly process. Antibody thermostability is one of the key developability features of an antibody drug that influences its chances of success in development. But, experimental testing such as nanoDSF for large libraries of candidates requires substantial resources. Instead, we evaluated an open-source feature-based machine learning workflow to train a model for antibody stability (Tm1) predictions from sequence and structure-based features. We used PROPERMAB to extract features from a selection of 231 different monoclonal and bispecific antibodies from the GDPa4 nanoDSF dataset. We benchmarked regression and classification models that predict the median first thermal transition temperature (Tm1) from PTS-IF in degrees Celsius for antibodies in the GDPa4 data set from Gingko Datapoints. We trained the models on 184 antibodies and evaluated model performance on 47 held-out antibodies. The three different regression models were ElasticNet, RandomForest, and GradientBoosting. RandomForest achieved the highest reported correlations among the regressors (Pearson r = 0.750, R2 = 0.562). Performance was also evaluated relative to 66.29 degrees Celsius as the threshold for thermostability. The classifier models were LogisticRegression, RandomForest, SupportVector, and GradientBoosting, and classification was defined relative to the training set median of 66.29 degrees Celsius. Thus, above-threshold and below-threshold describe position in this data set, not developability. The best performing model, RandomForest, improved on recall but reduced its precision by recovering two above-threshold antibodies in return for two more false positives. False positives are preferred to false negatives and classification models tended to reduce false negative counts. items.abstract: InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro) is a freely accessible resource for the classification of protein sequences. It integrates predictive models, known as signatures, from multiple member databases to classify sequences into families and to predict the presence of domains and functionally important sites. The InterPro database provides annotations for hundreds of millions of sequences, ensuring extensive coverage of UniProtKB, the standard repository of protein sequences, and includes mapping to several other major resources, such as Gene Ontology, the Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In this publication we report on the status of InterPro (version 110.0), detailing new developments in the database, its associated web interface, and software. Notable updates include InterPro-N, a deep-learning method that increases sequence coverage of UniProtKB to over 90%; the transition from InterProScan 5 to the completely re-engineered InterProScan 6; the integration of structure-based domain classifications and predicted structures from AlphaFold; a redesigned protein viewer offering a concise summary view; and a new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants to query InterPro programmatically. Over the past two years, 9484 new InterPro entries have been created, bringing the total to 54 922. InterPro data, software and tools are freely available.

items.abstract: Single-cell foundation models currently learn from gene count matrices, which are discretized, species-specific summaries that discard the RNA sequence, splice-site usage, 3 ′ UTR isoform identity and the mutational information present in the underlying sequencing reads. Here we introduce single-cell raw data pretraining, a framework that trains foundation models directly on sequencing reads, requiring no read alignment or count matrix, allowing any trained model to be applicable to arbitrary species. Our first model in this framework, the single-cell read model scRM, pairs two transformer encoders with a hierarchy of attention pools and contains 1.2 million parameters. We trained it as a JEPA on 3,000 mouse neuron cells on a single H100 in one hour, and benchmarked it zero-shot against leading single-cell foundation models with orders of magnitude more parameters and training cells. Our results show that our lightweight model reaches the performance of existing models on all tasks, and exceeds every one of them on perturbation detection tasks whose detection requires sequence-level detail. To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM .

items.abstract: Most single-cell studies measure either gene expression or chromatin accessibility, and connecting the two usually requires fitting a model to each study. Here we present MUTUAL (MUltiome Transfer in a Unified Aligned Latent space), which keeps the single-cell foundation models scFoundation and EpiAgent frozen, combines their embeddings with linear summaries of each modality and learns a shared RNA– ATAC space from 3.0 million paired cells of 400 public multiome datasets. Applied without refitting to ten datasets not used for training, MUTUAL matched cells’ RNA and ATAC profiles more accurately than methods fitted on other donors of the same dataset, annotated ATAC-only cells more accurately and transferred transcription-factor motif activity to RNA-only cells beyond what cell-type assignment provides. In a maturation series of stem-cell-derived islets, motif activity predicted from RNA largely reproduced the measured stage-wise changes when other libraries of the series served as the reference. MUTUAL makes public multiome data directly usable by single-modality studies.

items.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

items.abstract: Background Ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) are distinct diseases but may share fibroblast mediated mechanisms involving tissue remodeling and inflammation. However, their common molecular features at single cell resolution remain insufficiently defined. Methods We integrated single cell RNA sequencing datasets from ICM and LUAD with bulk transcriptomic profiles from TCGA LUAD, GSE18842, and GSE48166. Differential expression analysis identified 36 shared core genes. A total of 127 combinations of machine learning algorithms and feature selection methods were benchmarked to identify six hub genes: KRTCAP3, RUNX2, DBF4B, C11orf80, COL3A1, and ZFP64. UCell, scMetabolism, SCISSOR, Monocle 3, CellChat, scTenifoldNet/scTenifoldKnk, virtual drug screening, and molecular docking were used for functional characterization. Results Fibroblasts were the dominant cellular source of the six hub genes in both ICM and LUAD. COL3A1 progressively increased along fibroblast pseudotime trajectories. Virtual overexpression and knockout analyses showed convergence on extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory response, and immune regulation. Cell communication analysis identified fibroblasts as major senders of COLLAGEN signaling, with recipient cells shifting from inflammatory monocytes under normal conditions to proliferating macrophages in ICM and tumor cells in LUAD. Molecular docking nominated Digoxin, Ergotamine, and Ledipasvir as candidate RUNX2-binding compounds with favorable predicted docking scores. Conclusions This study provides a single cell framework linking ICM and LUAD through fibroblast driven extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammation, and identifies potential molecular targets and therapeutic candidates for further validation.

items.abstract: Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a widespread foodborne mycotoxin with hepatotoxic and immunotoxic effects, but its role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and antitumor immunity remains unclear. Here, we integrated network toxicology, bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, machine learning, molecular interaction assays, and experimental validation to identify key molecular factors associated with OTA-enhanced HCC progression. DNA topoisomerase II alpha (TOP2A) was prioritized, and direct OTA-TOP2A interaction was supported by surface plasmon resonance and drug affinity-responsive target stability assays. OTA increased TOP2A expression, promoted HCC-cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and suppressed apoptosis. TOP2A knockdown attenuated these effects, whereas shRNA-resistant TOP2A rescue substantially restored the malignant phenotypes. In HCC cell-T-cell coculture, OTA-pretreated tumor cells impaired CD8⁺ T-cell responses, as indicated by reduced CD69, granzyme B, and IFN-γ expression, increased PD-1 expression, and enhanced T-cell apoptosis. These effects were alleviated by TOP2A knockdown, and this alleviation was reversed by TOP2A rescue. CCK-8 and LDH release assays further showed that OTA pretreatment reduced CD8⁺ T-cell-associated cytotoxicity against Hep3B cells, whereas tumor-cell TOP2A knockdown attenuated this reduction and shRNA-resistant TOP2A rescue reversed the protective effect of knockdown. Direct OTA treatment of T cells alone did not produce comparable changes in the measured endpoints. Integrative transcriptomic analysis further revealed opposing metabolic programs between OTA exposure and TOP2A knockdown. Notably, glycolysis-related gene sets were positively enriched following OTA treatment but negatively enriched after TOP2A knockdown, accompanied by reciprocal regulation of glycolysis- and tumor microenvironment-associated genes, including LDHA, SLC2A1, PGK1, CA9, and SERPINE1. In an immunocompetent orthotopic HCC model, OTA promoted tumor growth and proliferative activity and reduced intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, whereas tumor-cell Top2a knockdown attenuated these effects. Collectively, these findings provide gene-specific evidence for a functional contribution of tumor-cell TOP2A to OTA-enhanced HCC progression and impaired CD8⁺ T-cell responses, including reduced antitumor cytotoxicity, while TOP2A-associated glycolytic alterations represent a potential downstream feature that requires further functional validation.

items.abstract: Pneumatosis intestinalis (PI) has a wide range of etiologies, and the imaging differentiation between benign and ischemic PI is difficult, leading to a high risk of missed diagnosis. This study systematically summarizes the CT (Computed Tomography) imaging manifestations of PI and constructs an AI (Artificial Intelligence)-assisted diagnostic model that integrates multidimensional features. This study retrospectively collected CT and x-ray data from 612 patients with PI (398 benign and 214 ischemic cases) from three tertiary hospitals, and included an external validation set of 106 cases. Imaging analysis established a five-level PI-CT severity scoring system based on gas morphology, distribution, portal venous gas (PVG), intestinal wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, and ascites. The AI system adopted a two-level architecture: The first level used EfficientNet-B3 for rapid screening on x-ray films; the second level used 3D nnU-Net (No-new-Net) to segment intestinal wall gas, and then fused the data through a three-branch network (gas morphology, accompanying signs, and clinical metadata) via cross-attention to output the probability of ischemic PI. In the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.947 for ischemic PI (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 93.6%), significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC = 0.876); the AUC on the external validation set was 0.931. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that PVG and blood lactate were the most important predictors. This two-tiered AI system can significantly improve the early identification of the causes of critical PI, providing a reliable method for intelligent diagnosis of emergency imaging.

items.abstract: We developed and evaluated a deep learning pipeline for skull-base synthetic computed tomography (sCT) generation from routine non-contrast T1-weighted and T2-weighted brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), focusing on clinically relevant bony anatomy for neurosurgical and radiotherapy workflows. We retrospectively collected 184 manually registered T1/T2/CT triplets for training and internal validation (166/18 split) and 43 cases from a second center for independent-center validation. A three-dimensional Swin-UNETR generator was trained with bone-weighted multiscale reconstruction, perceptual, and adversarial losses. Two board-certified radiologists independently scored 16 skull-base structures, artifacts, and diagnostic acceptability on raw sCT in Hounsfield units (HU), without histogram matching; this blinded review was the primary endpoint. Acceptability was 76.7% for Rater 1 and 67.4% for Rater 2 (pooled 72.1%, cluster-robust 95% CI 58.5-82.6%), with mean structure scores from 2.67 to 4.85 out of 5. Raw sCT showed limited absolute HU calibration (global MAE 364±50 HU, bone Dice 0.38±0.09 ), with a compressed dynamic range in which air and soft tissue were overestimated and dense bone underestimated; histogram-matched outputs, reported as a secondary analysis, reached bone Dice 0.88±0.03 and bone MAE 26.31±5.03 HU. Halo artifacts were near-universal, and false-canal artifacts occurred in 21-30% of cases. The method shows promise as a radiation-free adjunct for skull-base visualization, but the present results do not support replacing dedicated CT for diagnostic, dosimetric, or physics-based applications.

items.abstract: To synthesize the performance and methodological characteristics of fully automated deep learning algorithms for shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) segmentation. This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. CENTRAL, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception through July 17, 2026. The protocol specified fully automated deep learning-based pixel-wise segmentation of shoulder MRI, an expert-derived MRI-space reference standard, and quantitative segmentation metrics. Two reviewers independently screened records; unresolved disagreements were adjudicated by a senior reviewer. Overlapping datasets were linked during synthesis. Of 354 identified records, 169 duplicates were removed, 185 records were screened, and 53 full-text reports were assessed. Thirty-five reports were included (31 journal articles and 4 full conference papers; 2018-2026). U-Net-based encoder-decoder architectures predominated, with additional region-based, transformer, adversarial, and autoencoder approaches. Dice similarity coefficients ranged from approximately 0.81-0.99 for osseous targets, 0.71-0.99 for shoulder muscles, and 0.58-0.94 for tendon or tear regions; intersection-over-union values for tear or surgical-planning regions ranged from 0.45-0.83. MRI protocols and validation designs were heterogeneous, and most reports described retrospective single-center investigations. Five reports used independent external test sets; several others included multicenter images. Overlapping cohorts precluded a valid pooled participant count. Deep learning achieved high accuracy for shoulder bones and rotator-cuff muscles in selected datasets, whereas tear-region performance was more variable. Multicenter patient-level validation and standardized annotation and reporting are needed before routine clinical deployment.

items.abstract: Early neurological deterioration (END) affects approximately one in five patients with acute lacunar infarction and is associated with poor functional outcome. Hypoperfusion on contrast-enhanced perfusion MRI has been linked to END, but perfusion imaging requires intravenous contrast and is not part of the routine acute workup for minor stroke. We explored whether intensity features of non-contrast structural MRI carry information on END, using the visually classified pattern from a contrast-enhanced perfusion study in the same patients as a reference. We analyzed a prospectively collected single-center cohort of patients with acute lacunar infarction who underwent MRI within 24 h of symptom onset, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging. END was defined as an increase of ≥ 2 points on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale within 72 h. One hundred patients with complete imaging and outcome data were included, of whom 20 (20.0%) developed END. Candidate predictors comprised intensity features of the infarct core and an 8-mm perilesional rim normalized to whole-brain intensity, 201 DWI texture features, and 22 clinical and laboratory variables. Models were evaluated by 10-times-repeated 5-fold stratified cross-validation with the decision threshold fixed at 0.5; feature selection and standardization were performed within training folds only. The visually classified perfusion pattern served as a contrast-based clinical benchmark. ADC intensity features discriminated END with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.699 (approximate patient-level 95% CI 0.56-0.84) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.473 against a base rate of 0.200; at the fixed threshold, sensitivity was 52.0% and positive predictive value 27.9%. The perfusion pattern alone yielded a sensitivity of 70.0%, a specificity of 60.0% and a negative predictive value of 88.9% (balanced accuracy 0.650). The difference between the two predictors was small relative to the sampling uncertainty at 20 events, so neither superiority nor equivalence could be established. The strongest individual feature was the 75th percentile of normalized ADC within the infarct core (univariate AUC 0.702), with higher values in patients who deteriorated (median 0.615 versus 0.555, P = 0.005). Adding the perfusion pattern to the ADC features did not improve discrimination (AUC 0.665, 95% CI 0.645-0.684). The signal was confined to the ADC map: models built on DWI or FLAIR intensity alone performed below chance (AUC 0.463 and 0.453). More complex models did not reach the ADC model at this sample size: 201 DWI texture features reached an AUC of 0.566, clinical and laboratory variables at best 0.625, and an end-to-end 2.5D ResNet-18 0.404 with random initialization, 0.482 with ImageNet pretraining and 0.611 for a small network sized for the data. In this exploratory single-center study, ADC intensity features obtained without contrast were associated with END in acute lacunar infarction, with discrimination similar in magnitude to the contrast-enhanced perfusion benchmark; the cohort was too small to establish equivalence, and threshold-level performance is insufficient to guide monitoring. Texture analysis and deep learning could not be adequately trained with 20 events, so their relative merit cannot be judged. ADC appears to be the informative non-contrast sequence; the findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

items.abstract: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) presents challenges for computational tumor classification and localization because tumor appearance and surrounding anatomy vary across examinations. This work presents NeuroTürkNet, a two-stage prototype that combines a custom convolutional neural network (CNN) for four-category image classification with a YOLOv8n model for tumor-region localization. Input MRI images were resized to 640 × 640 pixels and processed using contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) and bilateral filtering. The classification dataset comprised 3,264 publicly sourced images, and the localization dataset comprised 5,858 annotated images. The CNN was trained with Adam optimization, class weighting, and validation-based learning-rate scheduling; the YOLOv8n component was trained separately and applied to images classified as tumor-bearing. In the detailed test results reported for the classifier, accuracy was 90.84%, precision 90.87%, recall 90.84%, F1-score 90.80%, and ROC-AUC approximately 0.99. The localization component reported an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.81, a best mAP@50 of 0.88, and best precision of 0.85. A graphical prototype supports MRI upload, visualization of predicted regions, and PDF output. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed computational workflow on the datasets described, but they do not establish clinical diagnostic validity. Independent validation and a complete audit of dataset partitions are needed before medical deployment.

items.abstract: Rationale and objectives Neurodegenerative Parkinson syndromes show regionally distinct tissue loss involving several brainstem and midbrain structures. Reliable volumetry is constrained by atlas-based segmentation in atrophy-affected brains. We developed a multiclass convolutional neural network (CNN) for the segmentation of 16 brainstem-related regions on routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Materials and methods In this retrospective single-center study, 200 manually annotated MRI datasets of patients with Parkinson's disease, atypical Parkinson syndromes, and healthy controls were used for model development and validation. A Deep Neural Patchwork model was trained on 150 datasets and evaluated in an independent test cohort of 50 participants against atlas-based segmentation using the Dice coefficient, 95% Hausdorff distance, and average symmetric surface distances (ASSD). In an extended validation cohort of 264 participants, CNN-derived regional volumes were analyzed across Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). Results CNN segmentation outperformed atlas-based segmentation across accuracy metrics. Overall medians were 0.75 vs 0.33 for Dice, 2.0 vs 5.0 mm for 95% Hausdorff distance, and 0.30 vs 1.02 mm for ASSD. CNN-derived volumetry recapitulated established disease-associated patterns, including predominant mesencephalic, superior cerebellar peduncle, and red nucleus atrophy in PSP and more marked pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle volume loss in MSA. Conclusion The principal contribution of this study is an atrophy-robust multiclass brainstem segmentation framework. This framework may enable anatomically more faithful extraction of quantitative MRI metrics than atlas-based approaches and may reduce contamination from adjacent CSF spaces, particularly in small atrophy-affected structures.

items.abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.

items.summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional…
items.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, 16.09times supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to 3.56times generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

items.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT
items.summary: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be…
items.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.

items.summary: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound…
items.abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.

items.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
items.summary: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website…
items.abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

items.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
items.summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048…
items.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

items.title: TaoMate-HD: Progressive-Resolution Autoregressive Audio-Video Generation
items.summary: Streaming digital humans produce detailed video while continuing speech as new text arrives. High-resolution denoising is costly, and text updates can cause repeated or interrupted speech. We present TaoMate-HD, an autoregressive model for high-resolution audio-video streaming. For each short segment, or chunk, two denoising steps establish coarse video structure at low resolution. A final step refines the video to…
items.abstract: Streaming digital humans produce detailed video while continuing speech as new text arrives. High-resolution denoising is costly, and text updates can cause repeated or interrupted speech. We present TaoMate-HD, an autoregressive model for high-resolution audio-video streaming. For each short segment, or chunk, two denoising steps establish coarse video structure at low resolution. A final step refines the video to high resolution, with audio generated throughout the same trajectory. Each stage passes its audiovisual predictions to the same stage of the next chunk as history. Across text updates, the model retains this history to infer what has already been spoken. Continuation training utilizes asymmetric text conditioning, with separate text windows for generation and distillation. Experiments show a 1.6x speedup over direct high-resolution generation with the same model and hardware. Optimized stage-parallel deployment provides a further 1.9x overall speedup over serial progressive generation. Our continuation training reduces character error rate by 11.18 percentage points relative to the baseline. The model also supports hour-long audiovisual generation. Our project page is https://taoliveaigc.github.io/TaoMate-HD.

items.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
items.summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive…
items.abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

items.title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
items.summary: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations,…
items.abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.

items.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
items.summary: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We…
items.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.

items.title: VidDub: Replacement-Aware Distillation for Two-Step Video Dubbing
items.summary: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired-audio samples…
items.abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio-visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present VidDub, a full-context diffusion editor distilled into two denoising steps (2 NFE). Our replacement-aware teacher first learns accurate lip synchronization without regressing toward conflicting source mouth movements. Matched trajectory regression then transfers the teacher's CFG-guided trajectories to a two-step student, and distribution matching distillation recovers visual quality after step compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833; the final two-step model combines strong lip synchronization with superior visual quality, identity preservation, and visual speech recognition across four benchmarks.

items.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
items.summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while…
items.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

items.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our…
items.abstract: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.
