items.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

items.title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
items.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. items.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96% of their own full-depth performance at 50% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.

items.abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. items.abstract: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

items.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
items.summary: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the…
items.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9times the success, 5.4times the generalization, and 3.9times the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8times faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.

items.abstract: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

items.abstract: Scientific names increasingly connect papers from different research topics, leaving readers to recover a paper's identity from context. We study this convergence in 564,861 AI-related arXiv records. Cross-topic name collision grows 4.33-fold from a pooled 2020-2022 reference to 2026, compared with 1.12-fold within topics. A second sentence encoder reproduces the pattern, and name-group resampling quantifies its uncertainty. Fixed word-frequency bands locate the main increase in an intermediate-frequency vocabulary shared by many research areas. We then measure the ambiguity that remains after supplying research clues. With the same three-term query construction, shared-name targets retain matched identification deficits of 25.7 percentage points under title-based BM25 and 6.9 points under title-plus-abstract E5. Within fixed same-name candidates, listwise language-model ranking reaches 89.2% using the query and candidate titles. Topic-specific comparisons show that context resolves more cross-topic ambiguity. The evaluation separates candidate competition, document fields, and contextual ranking through lexical, dense, and language-model baselines. Source-linked cases and a portable evaluation collection make the phenomenon inspectable and reusable for scientific retrieval and research assistants.

items.abstract: Endophytic fungi are non-pathogenic symbionts that represent a rich source of structurally diverse bioactive secondary metabolites. However, genome-mining studies reveal that most of their biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) remain transcriptionally silent under standard laboratory conditions, leaving much of their chemical diversity unexplored. This review examines antibacterial natural products from endophytic fungi by integrating three complementary aspects: metabolite chemistry, biosynthetic pathways, and strategies for activating cryptic BGCs. Endophytic fungi produce polyketides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenoids, phenylpropanoid-derived compounds, and hybrid metabolites with antibacterial activities mediated through inhibition of ribosomes, cell wall and membrane biosynthesis, and bacterial resistance mechanisms. Their genomes encode diverse PKS, NRPS, TPS, and hybrid biosynthetic systems, many of which remain cryptic. Advances in chemical elicitation, co-cultivation, epigenetic modulation, CRISPR-based engineering, genome mining, and machine learning are accelerating the activation of silent clusters and the assignment of BGCs to their metabolites. Several fungal metabolites exhibit potent activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including MRSA, and some enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. This review highlights current progress, identifies remaining challenges in metabolite production and BGC annotation, and outlines future directions for translating endophytic fungi into a sustainable platform for next-generation antibacterial drug discovery.

items.abstract: Designing selective kinase inhibitors is a multiobjective optimization problem constrained by the structural conservation of the human kinome, along with the lack of high-quality interaction data. Traditional deep learning methods often train complex neural networks directly on small datasets and fail to generalize to new chemical scaffolds. To this end, we present Geometric Manifold Alignment, a novel linear approach that shifts away from architectural complexity. We introduce Multi-View Linear Manifold (MVLM), which aligns the latent spaces of ChemBERTa (small molecules) and ESM-2 (protein sequences) into a shared geometric interaction space. We pretrain MVLM on the Universal Foundation Set of 473 923 high-confidence interactions, where binding affinity is represented as geometric proximity between drug and target embeddings. Achieving an AUROC of 0.936 on KIBA and 0.928 on Davis, MVLM establishes the new state-of-the-art on industry-standard benchmarks, outperforming existing methods (p < 0.001). In this work, interpretability is geometric where interaction scores are cosine similarities in a shared manifold, and the learned structure recovers kinase phylogenetic relationships without supervision. We also demonstrate the model's utility as a transparent discovery engine by retrieving known clinical targets of FDA-approved drugs. Our findings suggest that aligning pretrained chemical and biological representations provides a scalable and interpretable approach to advancing computational drug discovery.

items.abstract: The pharmaceutical sector is undergoing considerable transformation as a result of the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, robotics, and advanced computing technologies. Traditional pharmaceutical discovery and development processes can be lengthy, costly, and associated with high failure rates, thereby necessitating more efficient approaches. Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) combines autonomous decision-making, goal-oriented reasoning, adaptive learning, and multi-step task execution. These capabilities may increase the autonomy and coordination of pharmaceutical research workflows. At the same time, self-driving or autonomous laboratories that utilize robotics, machine learning, laboratory automation, and real-time data analytics to conduct experiments with minimal or no human intervention have emerged as an alternative approach. Agentic AI can provide a higher-level orchestration layer for autonomous laboratories, while established approaches such as Bayesian optimization, active learning, machine learning, and robotic experimentation provide many of the underlying capabilities required for closed-loop experimentation. These technologies can be applied to drug discovery, lead optimization, formulation development, process optimization, and personalized medicine. Several challenges related to data quality, transparency, regulation, cybersecurity, ethical considerations, and infrastructure must be addressed before these systems can be widely adopted. In addition, current evidence is dominated by computational studies, research-scale proof-of-concept platforms, and early industrial implementations. Substantial uncertainty remains regarding their reproducibility, scalability, and effects on overall drug development timelines. Rather than representing an established replacement for conventional pharmaceutical research, the convergence of Agentic AI and autonomous laboratories should currently be regarded as an emerging systems-level architecture that builds upon established approaches such as Bayesian optimization, active learning, robotic experimentation, and closed-loop optimization. Its potential value lies in extending autonomy from individual computational or experimental tasks toward coordinated research workflows, although the extent of this added value remains to be established through prospective and end-to-end validation. Accordingly, fully autonomous pharmaceutical research should be regarded as a long-term research objective rather than an established technological capability, with its realization dependent on further advances in scientific reasoning, experimental validation, regulatory governance, cybersecurity, and human-AI collaboration.

items.abstract: While there is an abundance of static data for the structure of biological macromolecules, the data regarding their folding mechanisms and dynamics is scarce, posing a challenge to the training of AI models. The World Model approach, which has been very successful in robotics, can come in handy in this regard. From limited data, it can build a latent, approximated representation of the spatio-temporal folding environment that can be used to train downstream AI models. Here, we developed DreamFold, a World Model-based generative framework to perform biomolecular simulations. DreamFold encodes protein structures and dihedral angle moves into latent vectors using variational autoencoders. Then, it uses another neural network to rapidly predict the next latent structure after a latent move, allowing the model to develop its own understanding of protein dynamics. Finally, in a "hallucinated" latent environment, an agent learns, through evolutionary algorithms, a policy to drive folding simulations toward a target. Latent configurations can then be decoded back into atomistic structures. DreamFold can compute protein folding pathways four orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD), up to ~30,000×. Furthermore, for the monomeric proteins tested here (up to 449 aa), the computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms (N) as O(N) (in comparison, MD scales as O(NlogN)). We have validated our results against established MD benchmarks and other available experimental data. Finally, we show how DreamFold allows us to identify folding intermediates with cryptic binding sites that are therapeutically valuable. Overall, DreamFold facilitates the study of protein dynamics by generative AI with applications in structure-based drug discovery.

items.abstract: Zymoseptoria tritici is a significant wheat pathogen responsible for Septoria tritici blotch (STB) disease. Despite its economic impact, understanding of the molecular interactions between Z. tritici and its host remains limited, particularly the functions of many uncharacterized candidate effectors. Here, we assessed seven Z. tritici candidate effectors with elevated expression during the early biotrophic phase and transition to necrotrophy by transiently expressing them in the heterologous, non-host system Nicotiana benthamiana, with and without their predicted signal peptides. AlphaFold structural predictions revealed that two candidates share similarity with proteins of known function: a sterol-binding protein from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and a necrosis-inducing effector from Valsa mali. Effector-associated phenotypes did not always correlate with expression timing, and signal peptide presence significantly influenced observed activities. Because N. benthamiana is not a natural host of Z. tritici, observed responses may reflect conserved, host-independent activities of effectors or immune recognition by N. benthamiana, rather than their native functions in wheat. Consistent with this distinction, two candidate effectors, Mycgr3107904 and Mycgr394290, induced cell death in N. benthamiana while also modulating reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, likely indicative of immune recognition. Some candidates attenuated ROS production, suggesting potential targeting of conserved cellular processes, whereas none suppressed PBR1-mediated cell death. Overall, our results indicate that candidate effector activities cannot be inferred from expression profiles alone, and that responses in the non-host N. benthamiana system reflect a combination of immune recognition and potential conserved activities, and primarily serve to prioritize candidates for validation in the native wheat-Z. tritici interaction.

items.abstract: Lacritin is an abundantly expressed glycoprotein in tear fluid and plays key roles in immune response, tear secretion, and bacterial killing. These biological functions are tightly regulated through several biochemical mechanisms including multimerization, proteolysis, and alternative splicing, especially within its C-terminal domain. Given its critical role at the ocular surface, lacritin is currently under investigation as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic candidate for dry eye disease (DED). However, despite over three decades since its initial discovery, the functional significance of the O-glycans that comprise more than 50% of its molecular weight remains largely unknown. To address this gap, we leveraged mass spectrometry (MS)-based glycoproteomics, AlphaFold 3.0, and molecular dynamics (MD) to explore the structural role of site-specific O-glycans on C-terminal lacritin. In doing so, we identified distinct glycosylation profiles between monomeric and multimeric lacritin, particularly at glycosites located near crosslinking residues (Lys101 and Lys104) that modulate multimer formation. Based on our glycoproteomics data, we performed MD simulations on monomer and multimer glycoforms and revealed that O-glycans may participate in intramolecular glycan-protein interactions that influence its structure and the spatial arrangement of Lys101 and Lys104. Differences in the solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and root mean squared fluctuation (RMSF) of these residues further suggested that proximal O-glycosylation could affect their ability to participate in crosslinking. To test these predictions, we performed in vitro crosslinking assays and demonstrated reduced TGM2-mediated multimerization of glycosylated versus unmodified lacritin. Finally, we show that recombinant glycoforms bearing O-glycan patterns similar to endogenous lacritin multimers are enriched after TGM2 crosslinking. Taken together, these findings underscore a central role for lacritin O-glycans in affecting structural topology and multimerization with implications for its downstream biological activity.

items.abstract: TYRO3, AXL, and MERTK, the TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), play roles in phagocytosis and negative regulation of immune responses, contributing to homeostasis in many adult tissues. Aberrant TAM signaling leads to diseases including autoimmune disorders, viral infection, inflammation, and cancer. Development of successful drugs targeting TAM receptors is hindered by incomplete knowledge of the receptor activation mechanism. Receptor dimerization is assumed to play a role, as seen for most RTKs. However, full biological responses require the TAM ligands to engage phosphatidylserine in an opposing cell or virus membrane, suggesting a more complex mechanism, possibly involving higher-order receptor oligomerization or clustering. Here, we present an X-ray crystal structure of the ectodomain of MERTK, which adopts a highly curved conformation with key interdomain boundaries stabilized by N-linked glycan moieties. We show that this MERTK extracellular region (ECR) forms a similar conformation in solution using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), which also suggests a flexible ECR. We compare these crystallographic and solution data for MERTK with SAXS and AlphaFold structural predictions for the other two TAM receptors. SAXS data confirm that each TAM ECR has a distinct curvature, with TYRO3 the most bent and AXL relatively straight. This leads us to speculate that these different ectodomain conformations guide receptor-specific functions. The MERTK X-ray crystal structure also suggests a head-to-tail intermolecular interaction between the Ig2 domain of one MERTK and the FNIIIb domain of a second that has intriguing parallels with interactions that have been proposed to regulate Eph receptor clustering.

items.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) poses a significant global health challenge due to its high recurrence rate and resistance to cisplatin. While DNA repair pathways contribute to chemoresistance, the role of scaffold proteins in stabilizing repair enzymes remains largely unexplored. This study aimed to elucidate the function of CCDC43 in cisplatin sensitivity and to identify a natural product targeting the CCDC43-PNKP axis. Bioinformatic analyses were conducted using bulk and single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic datasets. Molecular assays investigated the CCDC43-PNKP interaction and the impact of neferine on this axis. Xenograft models assessed the efficacy of combined neferine and cisplatin treatment. Machine learning identified CCDC43 as a key prognostic marker and driver of cisplatin resistance. CCDC43 was upregulated in OSCC epithelial cells and associated with poor survival. CCDC43 bound and stabilized PNKP by inhibiting ubiquitin-dependent degradation, thereby enhancing DNA repair and reducing cisplatin sensitivity. Through artificial intelligence-based virtual screening and experimental validation, neferine was found to disrupt the CCDC43-PNKP interaction, promoted PNKP degradation, increased cisplatin-induced DNA damage, and suppressed OSCC growth without acute toxicity. Collectively, the CCDC43-PNKP axis represents a critical therapeutic target in OSCC. Neferine is a promising ethnopharmacological agent capable of improving cisplatin sensitivity by targeting this pathway.

items.abstract: Background Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients, yet PD-specific biomarkers and prediction models remain limited. This study aimed to identify glycated peptide biomarkers associated with CVD in PD patients and develop a prediction model integrating glycated proteomics and clinical indicators using machine learning. Methods In Phase I, a matched discovery cohort (48 PD patients with CVD and 48 without CVD) was used to identify glycated peptides by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with glmnet used to prioritise candidate biomarkers. In Phase II, candidate biomarkers were quantified in a prospective internal derivation cohort (n = 240) and a multicentre external validation cohort (n = 102). The combined model was developed using F-test feature selection and elastic-net logistic regression. Its predictive performance was compared with three published cardiovascular risk models. Patients were stratified using a training-derived Youden cutoff. Results In the discovery cohort, 257 glycated peptides were differentially abundant between groups. Four candidate biomarkers were prioritised, and two peptides, GEAFTLK(g)ATVLNYLPK and K(g)QHLFVK, were retained in the final model together with six clinical indicators: phosphate, diabetes, total Kt/V, albumin, cardiac troponin T, and glycated albumin. The combined model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.784 in the training set, 0.781 in the internal testing set, and 0.822 in the external validation cohort, respectively. Using the training-derived cutoff of 0.373, higher 1-year CVD incidence was observed in the high-risk group in both validation cohorts. The combined model also achieved higher ROC-AUCs than the published cardiovascular risk models. Conclusion We developed and externally validated a PD-specific CVD prediction model by integrating glycated peptide biomarkers with clinical indicators, which may facilitate earlier risk stratification and targeted prevention.

items.abstract: Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient-specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology-related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline- and retrieval-augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training-data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning. With rigorous validation, transparent implementation, continual updating, and appropriate expert oversight, GenAI may augment oncologists' judgment, improve patient understanding and experience, streamline cancer care delivery, and advance personalized oncology.

items.abstract: Purpose To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. Development and validation methods The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. Potential applications The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

items.abstract: Background Extracting mandibular third molars is a common procedure that carries a risk of injury to the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN). Panoramic radiographs (PR) are commonly used for preoperative assessment of the mandibular third molars, but they are not very reliable for evaluating the relationship of the IAN. This systematic review aims to evaluate the accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) models in assessing the relationship between mandibular third molars and the IAN. Materials and methods We conducted systematic searches in MEDLINE (via PubMed), the Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus for studies published between January 2020 and April 2026. Eligible studies evaluated artificial intelligence systems that analyze panoramic radiographs to assess the relationship between mandibular third molars and the IAN, using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) or expert assessments as references. The studies had to report key diagnostic performance metrics. Two independent reviewers carried out study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessments using the QUADAS-2 tool. Results We included eleven studies with more than 9,700 patients. The AI models reviewed, including architectures such as ResNet, VGG, and YOLO, demonstrated promising diagnostic performance. Their accuracy ranged from 0.630 to 0.896, with sensitivity and specificity reaching up to 0.92 and 0.95, respectively. No single architecture was consistently superior, but AI models outperformed less experienced human observers in the studies that included this comparison. Validation against CBCT usually yielded more reliable performance metrics than validation based solely on expert opinion. Conclusions AI models show promise as decision-support tools in the radiographic assessment of the relationship between mandibular third molars and the inferior alveolar nerve on panoramic radiographs. However, variations in datasets, reference standards, and validation methods across studies mean that no single architecture can yet be considered superior. Larger, multicenter, prospective studies with external validation are necessary to confirm these systems' performance before they can be widely used in clinical practice.

items.abstract: Background In the growing field of interventional radiology, emerging technologies implement the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to help tackle growing demands for treatment. Due to the anatomical differences in animals, volunteers offer the most realistic training and testing scenario, however safety considerations restrict rapid prototyping of these new technologies. Simulators have been a key facilitator in the testing of new technologies among numerous medical engineering studies, but often lack the realism to reliably test AI. Purpose This proof-of-concept study presents methods to create or enhance hyper-realistic radiographic simulators that can effectively function with a medical-grade AI software. Methods Iron-filled plastic was used to three-dimensionally (3D) print a series of blocks of heights up to 30 mm. By analyzing the intensities generated by different thicknesses of plastic, anonymous fluoroscopic images were turned into height maps (lithophanes) and 3D-printed. A static scene from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was then 3D-printed and imaged with different presets using two different x-ray systems for mathematical analysis. Lithophanes were then used as a radiographic background to experimental and commercial interventional simulators to test Caranx Medical's TAVIPILOT AI. Finally, fluoroscopies from 5 3D-printed lithophanes were mixed with 5 real images and presented to 5 expert volunteers to establish their realism in a structured survey. Results The 3D-printed x-ray lithophanes test-plates' radiographic appearance was rated as "Adequate" to "Good" across all fields of the survey, with participants praising their realism. The test-plate was able to reliably recreate the TAVI scene in different x-ray systems, with joint-histogram correlation coefficients above 0.9, and global structural similarity above 0.8. The lithophanes were imaged as a standalone test plate and as a backing to dynamic TAVI interventional simulators; in both cases, TAVIPILOT AI responded to the simulator as if it was operating on a real anatomical image. Conclusions Lithophane plates present an easy-to-implement solution to recreate monoplane x-ray scenes, which can be deployed to test software at the point of care with minimal logistical, ethical, or safety concerns. This study opens the door for a new range of interventional simulators able to recreate human-like appearance to test AI, offering a non-exclusive alternative to patient volunteers and anonymous data.

items.abstract: Background Dynamic MRI reconstruction often requires accurate, fast, and low-latency algorithms that generalize across multiple applications, sampling schemes, and rates, without problem-specific parameter tuning. Existing methods either lack generalizability or require extensive parameter adjustment. Purpose To develop generalizable, low-latency MRI reconstruction algorithms based on low-rank (LR) and low-rank + sparse (L+S) models that are accurate, fast, and require minimal parameter tuning across diverse dynamic MRI settings. Methods We propose a novel Alternating Gradient Descent and Minimization (AltGDmin) approach for L+S matrix recovery from column-wise undersampled measurements, and extend it to a 3-level hierarchical L+S model for dynamic MRI. A few-shot (FS) learning modification (AGM-L+S-FS) is introduced to enable near low-latency reconstruction with per-frame processing time comparable to or faster than scan time. A simpler LR-only variant is also evaluated. Results The proposed algorithms were validated on 6 prospective and 12 retrospective dynamic MRI datasets, covering cardiac, speech, and abdominal applications, with Cartesian, pseudo-radial, radial, and spiral sampling schemes. Experiments demonstrate accurate reconstruction, generalizability across datasets and sampling rates, and low-latency performance. Detailed comparisons with state-of-the-art LR, L+S, low-latency, and unsupervised deep learning methods show superior or comparable performance. Conclusions Our AGM-L+S-FS approach provide generalizable, fast, and low-latency MRI reconstruction across multiple dynamic MRI applications and sampling schemes, without the need for problem-specific parameter tuning.

items.abstract: Background Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but amplifies noise, which can degrade diagnostic reliability. Recent studies have applied diffusion-based models to LDCT denoising and shown promising performance. However, many of these approaches require paired LDCT and normal-dose CT (NDCT) data or dose-specific retraining, and their reconstruction procedures are often strictly coupled to a predefined diffusion trajectory. Purpose This study proposes an optimization-based LDCT denoising framework that uses a pre-trained NDCT diffusion model as an image prior and can be applied across various dose levels without dose-specific retraining. Methods We formulate LDCT denoising as an optimization problem guided by a pre-trained score-based generative model (SGM) trained only on NDCT images. The Poisson data fidelity term enforces consistency with the measured projection data, whereas the score distillation sampling (SDS) term acts as a regularizer that guides the reconstruction toward the NDCT distribution learned by the pre-trained SGM. The denoised image is obtained by iteratively optimizing a projection-domain residual variable using the combined Poisson data fidelity gradient and SDS-based regularization gradient. Results The proposed method effectively suppressed noise while preserving fine anatomical structures across multiple dose levels using a single pre-trained diffusion model. Quantitative evaluations with respect to full-dose reference images and visual comparisons demonstrated competitive performance compared with supervised and self-supervised LDCT denoising baselines. Conclusions The results show that diffusion-based image priors can be leveraged across various low-dose levels within the proposed optimization-based denoising framework. Our work suggests that SDS-guided diffusion priors are a promising direction for LDCT denoising in data-limited settings.

items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed-set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open-set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. Purpose This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. Methods We propose a GCD framework integrating semi-supervised contrastive learning with global-local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross-instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine-grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. Results We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Conclusions Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open-set diagnostic AI.

items.abstract: Background Multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MC-MRI) enables detailed tissue characterization by acquiring multiple contrast-weighted images from the same anatomical region. Redundancy across contrasts can improve reconstruction from under-sampled data. However, conventional deep learning approaches rely on fully-sampled, contrast-aligned datasets, which require long acquisition times. Extended scanning durations not only increase patient burden but may also introduce physiological risks, limiting the practical adoption of accelerated MC-MRI in clinical settings. Purpose This study introduces Self-MF, a self-supervised MC-MRI reconstruction framework that leverages contrast redundancy without requiring fully sampled target-contrast labels. The framework aims to provide a high-fidelity, scalable solution for reconstructing under-sampled multi-contrast images while preserving anatomical details and contrast fidelity. Methods Self-MF implements a contrast-aware self-supervised learning strategy that randomly partitions the acquired target k-space into input and held-out subsets, allowing the model to learn joint anatomical priors from under-sampled data without fully sampled target-contrast labels. A mask-guided frequency-domain conditioning module constructs reference-conditioned auxiliary frequency channels from auxiliary contrasts and acquired target measurements, enhancing the recovery of fine structural features during score-based reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on public datasets (IXI, fastMRI) and a clinical multi-coil dataset (SIAT), spanning multiple acceleration factors and undersampling patterns to assess robustness and generalizability. Results Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that Self-MF outperforms existing representative reconstruction methods across different contrasts, datasets, and acceleration factors. On the SIAT multi-contrast dataset, Self-MF achieved PSNR/SSIM values of 35.16/0.8870, 33.46/0.9054, and 35.31/0.9187 for T1WI, T2WI, and PDWI reconstruction under 2D random undersampling at R = 4, respectively. On the fastMRI brain dataset, Self-MF achieved 41.15 dB/0.9637 and 35.02 dB/0.8814 for T2WI reconstruction under R = 4 and R = 8, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared classical, learning-based, and diffusion-based baselines. Conclusions Self-MF provides an effective, self-supervised solution for high-fidelity MC-MRI reconstruction without fully sampled target-contrast labels. By combining contrast-aware self-supervision, frequency-domain conditioning, and diffusion-based reconstruction, the framework achieves superior image quality and robust anatomical preservation, representing a significant advancement for multi-contrast MRI in both research and clinical practice.

items.abstract: Background Computed Tomography (CT) provides geometric accuracy and electron density information essential for radiotherapy planning; however, it offers limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) improves tumor visualization but introduces registration uncertainties when acquired separately from the radiotherapy planning CT (pCT). Cross-modality image synthesis enables the generation of synthetic MRI (sMRI) directly from pCT and may combine the strengths of both modalities, reducing reliance on MRI access. Purpose We propose a two-stage deep-learning framework for generating sMRI from pCT image-sets specifically in head-and-neck (H&N) cancers, providing soft-tissue contrast comparable to ground-truth MR images (gtMRI). Methods This study included 60 patient cases with H&N cancer treated with radical radiotherapy between March 2022 and April 2024 for model development (50 for training, 10 for validation), plus 10 additional cases, independent of the development cohort for testing. All patients underwent a standard, non-contrast pCT scan followed by an MRI acquired on a 3T Siemens MR simulator. Images were deformably-registered, yielding 10,000 matched CT-MRI slice-pairs for model training. The proposed model utilizes a two-stage architecture, a Pix2Pix conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) for coarse sMRI synthesis, followed by a conditional diffusion model for refinement. To test the model's robustness, 10 patient cases with both pCT and contrast-enhanced CT (ceCT) were used to generate sMRI. Model performance was assessed using structural similarity index (SSIM), multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM), mean absolute error (MAE), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). In addition, the geometric agreement of the primary (GTVp_70) and nodal (GTVn_70) gross tumor volumes delineated on sMRI vs. gtMRI was independently assessed by two radiation oncologists (ROs) using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95 th -percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). Results The average MS-SSIM, SSIM, MAE and PSNR for pCT-derived sMRI were 0.82 ± 0.02, 0.70 ± 0.03, 0.05 ± 0.01, and 20.42 ± 0.66 dB, respectively. The mean MS-SSIM and SSIM values for ceCT-derived sMRI were 0.02 lower than those for the corresponding pCT-to-sMRI metrics. For the contour-based evaluation, sMRI-derived GTV contours achieved a mean DSC of 0.56 and 0.60 for GTVp_70, and 0.72 and 0.74 for GTVn_70 across the two ROs, relative to gtMRI contours. Conclusion Our proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of pCT-derived sMRI for H&N cancers using a deep-learning framework. The model produces grayscale patterns and soft-tissue contrast that closely resemble the gtMRI.

items.abstract: Background Lower‑field 0.55 T MRI scanners with large‑bore design could offer patients more comfortable feeling and flexible position. With the advances in deep‑learning reconstruction and hardware optimization, 0.55T have greatly improved their image quality and cost‑effectiveness for musculoskeletal applications. However, its feasibility for shoulder evaluation remains unstudied. Purpose To evaluate the image quality of shoulder using 0.55T MRI in volunteers and patients with rotator cuff injury with comparison of conventional 1.5T. Methods Fifty participants (25 volunteers, 25 patients) were prospectively enrolled. All participants underwent shoulder MRI both at open 0.55T with contour coils and deep learning (DL) and 1.5T MR without DL. The nonparametric method was utilized to compare image quality scores and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (|CNR|)). Arthroscopy have been conducted in 16 patients. Kappa statistics was used to assess interobserver and interstudy agreement for lesion evaluation. Comfort feeling was also compared. Results The scan time was 11'25″ for 0.55T MRI and 11'42″ for 1.5T MRI. The interobserver analyses showed high consistency (κ = 0.771-1.000, P: 0.008 ∼ < 0.001) among 3 readers. The scores for coronal fat suppressed T2 weighted imaging (fsT2WI) and coronal T1 weighted imaging (T1WI) were significantly higher for 0.55T MRI. Most sequences at 0.55T demonstrated significantly higher SNRs (P:0.04 ∼ < 0.001). Additionally, |CNR| values for lesions were significantly higher in fs proton weighted imaging (PDWI) and fsT2WI at 0.55T. Perfect interstudy agreement between 0.55T and 1.5T was observed between 2 readers (Kappa = 1, P < 0.001) for lesion assessment. Agreement between MRI findings and arthroscopic results was perfect or good. The 0.55T system received higher scores in comfort ratings. Conclusion The 0.55T MRI with DL, showed comparable or better image quality in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury to 1.5T MRI without DL.

items.abstract: MRpro is an open-source framework for MR image reconstruction and quantitative parameter estimation, with particular relevance to low-field MRI. Built on PyTorch, it supports modern deep-learning reconstructions and standardized data exchange through ISMRMRD for raw k-space data and DICOM and NIfTI for reconstructed images and parameter maps. This facilitates integration into existing pipelines and the use of data from different devices. MRpro provides unified data structures for the consistent manipulation of MR datasets and associated metadata, together with a library of composable operators, proximable functionals, and optimization algorithms. The operator library includes a unified Fourier operator for all common trajectories and operators specifically developed for low-field applications, such as a B 0 -correction operator. Together, these components underpin ready-to-use implementations of key reconstruction algorithms. For deep learning, MRpro includes data-consistency layers, differentiable optimization layers, state-of-the-art backbone networks, and access to public datasets to facilitate reproducibility. Automated quality control supports collaborative development. We demonstrate MRpro for automatic reconstruction, iterative SENSE, deep-learning-based reconstruction, and quantitative parameter estimation. For selected Cartesian and non-Cartesian tasks, iterative SENSE reconstructions from MRpro differed from those obtained with BART, SigPy, and MRIReco by less than 3% relative RMSE. Further applications use public and simulated datasets and measured low-field data acquired at 0.3 T, 0.6 T, and 47 mT. MRpro provides a reproducible and maintainable foundation for future MR imaging research.

items.abstract: Obtaining high-resolution brain MRI in small animals is challenging due to the inherent trade-off between image quality and acquisition time. Deep learning-based reconstruction (DLR) has emerged as a solution to improve image quality without prolonging scan time; however, its clinical utility and potential risks, such as pseudolesions, remain insufficiently evaluated in veterinary patients. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of DLR on lesion assessment and image quality in canine brain MRI and to investigate potential limitations associated with its application. This retrospective study compared DLR with conventional reconstruction in 25 canine brain MRI examinations diagnosed with intracranial diseases. Transverse T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were reconstructed using both conventional and DLR methods. Quantitative analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and lesion edge sharpness. Two blinded radiologists assessed image quality, lesion conspicuity, artifacts, pseudolesions, and lesion masking. DLR images exhibited significantly higher SNR, CNR, and lesion edge sharpness than conventional images in both sequences (p < 0.05). DLR images also yielded significantly higher qualitative scores for image quality and lesion conspicuity (p < 0.05). Truncation artifact was significantly reduced, whereas motion and pulsation artifacts showed no improvement. No instances of pseudolesions or lesion masking were noted. DLR significantly improves image quality and lesion conspicuity in canine brain MRI and reduces truncation artifacts; however, it does not mitigate motion or pulsation interference. Collectively, these findings suggest that DLR has potential value for improving image quality and lesion visibility in canine brain MRI, whereas further studies are needed to determine its impact on diagnostic performance.

items.abstract: Commonly occurring fat-water swap artifacts in multi-echo MRI hinder accurate estimation of the clinical biomarker, proton density fat fraction (PDFF). This study evaluates a novel physics-informed deep learning (PI-DL) model to correct these swap artifacts. The proposed PI-DL model, the "Swap-Net," utilizes a branch-constrained optimization method to explore different bifurcate regions in the residual function optimized, thereby increasing the probability of reaching global minima, as the swap artifacts are caused by the optimization routine settling into a local minimum. Performance evaluation was conducted using multi-echo MRI of 37 (n = 37) subjects, and this included a cohort of 23 (n = 23) high-resolution MRIs. The proprietary mDixon Quant sequence, with optimized parameter settings for accurate liver fat quantification, served as the clinical standard for benchmarking performance. The results of the quantitative evaluations revealed that the average liver PDFF% from the proposed Swap-Net demonstrated excellent agreement with the clinical standard mDixon Quant (correlation coefficient R of 0.98 in the high-resolution cohort). The qualitative evaluations also showed that the fat-water maps from the Swap-Net contained no swap artifacts. In contrast, other state-of-the-art methods exhibited swap artifacts, particularly in high-resolution MRI. The proposed Swap-Net corrected swap artifacts in MRI-based fat quantification, particularly in high-resolution MRI, enabling high-resolution fat-water imaging.

items.abstract: Purpose To investigate whether selective removal of vascular structures can improve lesion visibility and interpretability in maximum intensity projection (MIP) images derived from dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI. Materials and Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted using breast MRI scans from the Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI dataset for model development. Deep Learning-based Vessel sEgmentation and eraSure in Breast MRI (DeepVEST), a deep learning method for automatic vessel segmentation and removal, was developed. A reader study with five breast radiologists was conducted to evaluate the effect of vessel-removed MIPs on lesion assessment, using images from the Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI and Advanced-MRI-Breast-Lesions datasets. Segmentation performance was evaluated against manually annotated vessel segmentations using the Dice similarity coefficient, and perceived usefulness and quality were measured through reader study metrics. Interreader agreement on vessel removal quality and artifact impact was calculated using the Gwet agreement coefficient. Results DeepVEST achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.611 for vessel segmentation. In the reader study (150 assessments, 600 responses), vessels partially or fully obscured lesion margins in 91 of 150 assessments (60.7%). Vessel removal effectiveness was rated 3.820 ± 0.749 on a 5-point Likert scale. Artifacts were reported in 45 of 150 assessments (30.0%), with a low mean severity score of 0.493 ± 0.900 (scale of 0-5), indicating minimal effect of image quality. Substantial interreader agreement was observed for vessel removal quality (Gwet agreement coefficient of 0.703) and artifact evaluation (Gwet agreement coefficient of 0.736). Conclusion The DeepVEST method enabled automatic vessel segmentation and removal on breast MR MIP images, showing high effectiveness with minimal artifacts. Most readers found it helpful for lesion assessment in challenging cases. Keywords: Segmentation, Breast, Neural Networks, Image Postprocessing, MR-Imaging, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Breast MRI, Deep Learning, Vessel Segmentation, Vessel Removal, Reader Study Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026 See also the commentary by Tayebi Arasteh in this issue.

items.abstract: Objective To systematically examine different clinical data modalities in large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and to quantify the contribution of data modalities in early inpatient risk prediction and decision support tasks. Materials and methods We conducted a systematic analysis using MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR-JPG datasets to create a unified cohort of 22 254 hospital admissions containing structured electronic health records (EHRs), radiology reports (clinical notes), and chest X-ray images. We evaluated general-purpose and medical-adapted LLM/VLMs across uni-, bi-, and tri-modal configurations on 2 risk prediction tasks (in-hospital mortality and length of stay [LOS] prediction) and 2 clinical decision support (CDS) tasks (discharge diagnosis phenotyping and medication-use prediction). Results For risk prediction tasks, structured EHR data alone achieved the best or comparable performance (best mortality AUROC: 0.849; LOS AUROC: 0.868), with limited incremental benefit observed from adding radiology reports or medical images. For CDS tasks, multimodal integration yielded substantial improvements: the best tri-modal configuration achieved F1-scores of 0.589 (diagnosis) and 0.405 (medication), representing 21.4% and 18.4% improvement over the best unimodal approach. Radiology reports consistently outperformed raw single-view chest radiographs as a supplementary modality. MLLMs demonstrated better zero- and few-shot performance than unimodal LLMs. Multi-view imaging consistently improved performance over single view across all tasks. Conclusion The benefits of multimodal data integration are task dependent. Healthcare LLMs should examine clinical data modalities according to specific tasks for efficient integration. These findings provide practical guidance for designing efficient clinical decision support systems.

items.abstract: Seed implant brachytherapy (SIBT) is an effective cancer treatment modality; however, clinical planning often relies on manual adjustment of objective function weights, leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal results. This study proposes an adaptive weight optimization framework for SIBT planning, driven by large language models (LLMs). A locally deployed DeepSeek-R1 LLM is integrated with an automatic planning algorithm in an iterative loop. Starting with fixed weights, the LLM evaluates plan quality and recommends new weights in the next iteration. This process continues until convergence criteria are met, after which the LLM conducts a comprehensive evaluation to identify the optimal plan. A clinical knowledge base, constructed and queried via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), enhances the model's domain-specific reasoning. The proposed method was retrospectively validated on 23 patient cases who underwent head-and-neck SIBT, showing that the LLM-assisted approach maintained clinical target volume (CTV) coverage and reduced excessive target dose relative to fixed-weight planning; in the eight patients with available organs at risk (OARs) contours, OAR dose metrics showed favorable numerical trends. The study demonstrates the potential of LLMs as assistive tools for SIBT planning under clinician supervision.

items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects social interaction and behaviour in children. Current diagnostic methods largely depend on clinical observation and standardized assessments, which can be subjective, time-intensive and influenced by the experience of evaluator. Here, STWO_GDSNet is devised for detecting ASD. Firstly, input image is sent to image pre-preparation, where image is denoised by anisotropic diffusion Kuwahara filtering (ADKF), followed by N4 bias field correction. Next, based on functional connectivity, the pivotal region is extracted by STWO that combines supercell thunderstorm algorithm (STA) and leaf in wind optimization (LiWO). After that, multiscale triangle descriptor (MTD) is extracted in descriptor computation phase. Subsequently, the input autism data are pre-prepared by normalization and standardization. Next, analysis of variance (ANOVA) method conducts attribute pruning, and extracted features as well as the pruned data are passed to gated dual-stream convolutional neural network (GDSNet) for detecting ASD. Here, GDSNet is trained by STWO that incorporates STA and LiWO. The efficacy of STWO_GDSNet is examined by considering accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, which yield maximal values of 96.24%, 95.99% and 96.61%.

items.abstract: Bone-implant and scaffold research is beginning to use machine learning (ML) alongside biomaterials design and advanced manufacturing, but the literature is scattered across different material classes and stages of development. We therefore reviewed ML studies relevant to composite, multiphase, coated, graded, and multimaterial systems and organized them using the process-structure-property-performance (PSPP) sequence. PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus were used as the formal bibliographic databases; IEEE Xplore screening, targeted OpenAlex searches, and Google Scholar citation chasing provided supplementary coverage. The frozen dataset contained 46 primary studies. Twenty-five satisfied a strict composite/multimaterial definition, whereas 21 were retained as boundary-supporting evidence for the sensitivity analysis. The studies show that ML is being used for property prediction, surrogate modeling, inverse design, multi-objective optimization, and material screening. Validation, however, did not advance at the same pace as modeling. Physical or experimental confirmation was identified in 32/46 studies (69.6%), in vitro or in vivo experiments, including antibacterial assays, in 11/46 (23.9%), and external validation in only 2/46 (4.3%); none reported prospective clinical validation. Explicit uncertainty analysis and strong reproducibility were also uncommon. Taken together, the literature suggests that the main challenge is no longer demonstrating that an ML model can fit a biomaterials dataset. The more difficult task is showing that a model-guided choice remains useful after fabrication and biological testing. Priorities therefore include better-described multimodal datasets, independent and leakage-resistant validation, characterization of the manufactured rather than only nominal structure, uncertainty-aware design, physics-informed modeling, and prospective biological testing.

items.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a highly invasive malignancy associated with poor prognosis. However, reliable molecular subtypes and prognostic signatures for LUAD, particularly their associations with tumor immunity and treatment response, remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to identify distinct molecular subtypes and establish a robust prognostic signature for LUAD, while exploring potential therapeutic targets associated with cisplatin resistance. In this study, we integrated ten clustering algorithms with 101 machine learning methods to identify two distinct molecular subtypes of LUAD and established a robust consensus machine learning-derived signature (CMLS). Patients belonging to the Cluster A subtype exhibited a more favorable prognosis and an enhanced immune response. Furthermore, a CMLS model constructed from 19 genes exhibited strong predictive power. Individuals with high CMLS scores displayed reduced CD4 + T-cell infiltration, poorer survival outcomes, and diminished responses to immunotherapy, whereas those with the low CMLS scores showed improved clinical outcomes, better immunotherapy responsiveness, and features of an immunologically "hot" tumor phenotype. Among the identified genes, ribonucleotide reductase subunit M2 (RRM2) emerged as a core regulator associated with LUAD prognosis. RRM2 was markedly upregulated in lung cancer tissues and the LUAD cell lines and was associated with the cisplatin (DDP) resistance. Suppression of RRM2 expression significantly enhanced the cisplatin sensitivity of A549/DDP cells. In summary, our findings establish a molecular classifier that stratifies LUAD patients into distinct risk categories and highlight RRM2 as a promising biomarker and therapeutic target associated with cisplatin resistance.

items.abstract: Predicting postoperative complications is a critical task for improving patient care and optimizing resource management. We formulate the task as a binary classification problem based on two-stage clinical data: preoperative and intraoperative variables. A key difficulty is that intraoperative data are systematically missing for preoperative prediction. Existing methods, which typically rely solely on preoperative data or single intraoperative indicator imputation, generally fail to capture important latent intraoperative information. To provide a more robust solution, we propose P4MC (Preoperative, Partial intraoPerative, and Postoperative Monte Carlo classification). This approach explicitly models the dependence between the two stages to recover latent intraoperative information. Specifically, P4MC first applies partial sufficient dimension reduction (PSDR) to compress intraoperative variables into a low-dimensional sufficient reduction. We then estimate the conditional distribution of this reduction given preoperative variables using nonparametric density estimation and generate latent intraoperative features for classification via Monte Carlo sampling. A simulation study demonstrates the improved predictive performance and stability of P4MC when combined with standard machine learning methods. Applications to two clinical cohorts, laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy and hepatocellular carcinoma, further show that P4MC outperforms conventional approaches and yields clinically interpretable insights. An open-source R program is provided in the P4MC package, available at https://github.com/501fox/P4MC.git.

items.abstract: Background/aim This study aimed to develop a classification tree model to predict clinical complete response (cCR) after definitive hypofractionated RT in elderly patients with non-melanoma (basal and squamous cell carcinoma) skin cancer based on pre-treatment clinical parameters. Patients and methods Data from elderly patients (aged ≥ 70 years) with histologically proven non-melanoma skin cancer lesion(s) were reviewed. All lesions were treated with definitive hypofractionated RT. A decision tree methodology was applied to define significant pre-treatment parameters influencing the cCR rate. The data set included seven predictor variables (location, histology, T stage, diameter, bleeding, pain, previous treatment) and a dependent variable (cCR). The analysis was conducted using open-source R software. Important explanatory variables were selected using the random forest approach. A classification tree that optimally partitioned patients according to cCR was then built. Results A total of 121 patients with 145 non-melanoma skin cancer lesions were identified between January 2015 and December 2023. The cCR rate after treatment was 78.6%. The three most important variables identified were T stage, location and pain at diagnosis. Based on these explanatory variables, patients were partitioned in five groups. Of these groups, three experienced cCR rates ranging from 69% to 88% and two experienced cCR rates lower than 15%. Conclusion The proposed classification tree could serve as a valuable tool to guide future research in the field of non-melanoma skin cancer. The decision tree method may be an effective approach to partition elderly patients with non-melanoma skin cancer based on key clinical parameters.

items.abstract: Accurately measuring clinician fidelity to psychosocial evidence-based interventions (EBIs) is essential to advance equitable EBI implementation. Observational measures of live or recorded therapy sessions are widely considered the most reliable and valid metrics for indexing fidelity. However, they are costly, time and resource intensive, and rarely used in underresourced clinical settings; this makes it challenging to assess the quality of care delivered to underserved populations. Further, many fidelity coding schemes originated from clinical trials testing relatively structured clinical protocols with primarily White, middle-class individuals. This raises equity considerations for their use and interpretation in settings serving individuals with diverse identities and adverse social determinants of health, where flexible EBI application is often required to meet needs. For example, fidelity coding schemes do not always consider patient cultural and contextual factors that may lead clinicians to "stray" from fidelity standards. Guided by the health equity implementation framework, we outline key equity considerations related to observational fidelity measurement and interpretation in mental health. We describe several ongoing efforts to equitably assess fidelity to psychosocial EBIs in underresourced community settings using a variety of strategies including standardized patient paradigms codeveloped with community partners, snapshot coding of session recordings, artificial intelligence models that automate fidelity score generations, and leveraging expert consultation encounters to generate actionable fidelity data. We conclude by discussing implications for future research. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Compliance by Design: Governing AI-Augmented Quantitative Analysis in Clinical and Translational Research.
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from promise to routine practice in clinical and translational research, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to scope analyses, draft and debug code, and accelerate the quantitative work that supports clinical and translational decisions. items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from promise to routine practice in clinical and translational research, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to scope analyses, draft and debug code, and accelerate the quantitative work that supports clinical and translational decisions. This adoption is outpacing the operational safeguards that keep such work reproducible and auditable, and the central risk is not only erroneous code but the quieter erosion of the analytical discipline on which trustworthy bench-to-bedside decisions depend. In this position paper, we argue that AI can be integrated into regulated quantitative workflows without sacrificing reproducibility, provided it operates inside a compliance-by-design architecture built on two principles: analytical intent must be formally encoded and locked before execution, and the analysis itself must run outside the LLM as specification-verified code in a validated environment. We describe three failure modes that ordinary quality control does not detect, namely context drift, the displacement effect, and implementation drift, and we link each to documented model behavior. For open-ended investigation, these principles are operationalized as a four-step execution firewall; for recurring development studies such as assay validations and animal safety studies, they are operationalized through a governed library of documented, validated agents, supported by fit-for-purpose validation, a clear separation of human and machine roles, and post-deployment monitoring. Both approaches can be implemented with components available today. Used this way, AI enhances rather than replaces quantitative expertise, which now resides less in the code a model produces than in the constraints a scientist defines before it runs.

items.abstract: Background Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. Aim This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. Study design Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. Results Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. Conclusions Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. Relevance to clinical practice By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.
